fr:mainmatter.html:p: Because the type \overline {\mathcal {D}}_{f}{\mathopen {}\left (\overline {x} , \overline {y}\right )\mathclose {}} of displayed morphisms depends on the base morphism f, the two sides of each displayed law inhabit different displayed hom-sets — those indexed by the two sides of the corresponding base-category equation. Each displayed law is therefore a heterogeneous equality a =_{p} b: a path from a to b lying over the base path p, rather than an equation within a single fixed set.
Concretely, this definition models the one used in the Cubical standard library [cubicalagdalib].

A displayed category is to a category as a dependent type is to a context. In this way, displayed categories are effectively dependent categories, as we present the structure of \overline {\mathcal {D}} as a category parametrized by the structure of \mathcal {C}.

Displayed categories were introduced by Ahrens and Lumsdaine [ahrens-lumsdaine-2019]. The point is that a displayed category over \mathcal {C} is equivalent to the data of a category \mathcal {D} together with a functor F : \mathcal {D} \to \mathcal {C}, but presented as families indexed by the objects and morphisms of \mathcal {C} — so that constructions like Grothendieck fibrations can be defined without ever invoking equality of objects.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Cubical Agda Library
Displayed Categories
fr:frontmatter.fr:meta: @article{ahrens-lumsdaine-2019, author = {Ahrens, Benedikt and Lumsdaine, Peter LeFanu}, url = {https://lmcs.episciences.org/5252}, year = {2019}, month = mar, doi = {10.23638/LMCS-15(1:20)2019}, eprint = {1705.04296}, eprinttype = {arXiv}, issue = {1}, journal = {Logical Methods in Computer Science}, title = {Displayed Categories}, volume = {15}, }

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We introduce and develop the notion of displayed categories. A displayed category over a category C is equivalent to “a category D and functor F : D \to C, but instead of having a single collection of “objects of D” with a map to the objects of C, the objects are given as a family indexed by objects of C, and similarly for the morphisms. This encapsulates a common way of building categories in practice, by starting with an existing category and adding extra data/properties to the objects and morphisms. The interest of this seemingly trivial reformulation is that various properties of functors are more naturally defined as properties of the corresponding displayed categories. Grothendieck fibrations, for example, when defined as certain functors, use equality on objects in their definition. When defined instead as certain displayed categories, no reference to equality on objects is required. Moreover, almost all examples of fibrations in nature are, in fact, categories whose standard construction can be seen as going via displayed categories. We therefore propose displayed categories as a basis for the development of fibrations in the type-theoretic setting, and similarly for various other notions whose classical definitions involve equality on objects. Besides giving a conceptual clarification of such issues, displayed categories also provide a powerful tool in computer formalisation, unifying and abstracting common constructions and proof techniques of category theory, and enabling modular reasoning about categories of multi-component structures. As such, most of the material of this article has been formalised in Coq over the UniMath library, with the aim of providing a practical library for use in further developments.

A displayed bicategory \overline {\mathcal {K}} over a base bicategory \mathcal {K} mirrors the structure of \mathcal {K} field-for-field, one displayed level up. It is to a bicategory exactly as a displayed category is to a category.

A displayed bicategory over \mathcal {K} consists of
A type of displayed 0-cells \overline {x} lying over each 0-cell x : \mathcal {K}_{0}.
For displayed 0-cells \overline {x} and \overline {y} over x and y, a displayed category \overline {\mathcal {K} {\mathopen {}\left (x , y\right )\mathclose {}}} lying over the hom-category \mathcal {K} {\mathopen {}\left (x , y\right )\mathclose {}}. Its displayed objects are the displayed 1-cells \overline {f} : \overline {x} \to _{f} \overline {y} lying over 1-cells f : x \to y; its displayed morphisms are the displayed 2-cells \overline {\alpha } lying over 2-cells \alpha : f \Rightarrow g.
For each \overline {x}, a displayed identity 1-cell 1_{\overline {x}} lying over 1_{x}, packaged as a displayed functor over the base identity functor.
For displayed 0-cells \overline {x}, \overline {y}, \overline {z}, a displayed composition functor lying over the base composition functor \mathcal {K}_{\star }^{x,y,z}. It sends displayed 1-cells \overline {f} : \overline {x} \to _{f} \overline {y} and \overline {g} : \overline {y} \to _{g} \overline {z} to a horizontal composite \overline {f} \star \overline {g} lying over f \star g.
A displayed left unitor \overline {\lambda }, right unitor \overline {\rho }, and associator \overline {\alpha }: displayed natural isomorphisms lying over the base \lambda , \rho , and \alpha . Their components are invertible displayed 2-cells; for instance \overline {\alpha }_{\overline {f}, \overline {g}, \overline {h}} lies over the base associator component \alpha _{f,g,h}.
Displayed triangle and pentagon coherences: heterogeneous equalities between the relevant composites of displayed 2-cells, each lying over the corresponding base coherence law.

The recursion is the point: a displayed bicategory replaces each hom-category of \mathcal {K} by a displayed category over it, and each structural functor, natural isomorphism, and equation of \mathcal {K} by its displayed counterpart. Because the displayed coherences are heterogeneous equalities valued in sets of displayed 2-cells, they hold automatically for locally thin or otherwise prop-constrained instances.

Just as a displayed category is effectively a dependent category, a displayed bicategory is effectively a dependent bicategory: the structure of \overline {\mathcal {K}} is presented as a bicategory parametrized by the structure of \mathcal {K}, with no reference to a total bicategory or a projection down to it.

For categories \mathcal {C} and \mathcal {D}, we can define the weakening of \mathcal {D} over \mathcal {C} as a displayed category over \mathcal {C} which trivially displays a copy of \mathcal {D} over each object of \mathcal {C}.

Given a displayed category \overline {\mathcal {C}} over a category \mathcal {C} and another displayed category \overline {\mathcal {D}} over \int \overline {\mathcal {C}}, the total category of \overline {\mathcal {C}}, we can define \overline {\int } \overline {\mathcal {D}}, the displayed total category of \overline {\mathcal {D}}, as a displayed category over \mathcal {C}.
Given a functor F : \mathcal {C} \to \mathcal {D}, we can define a displayed category of fibers along F up to isomorphism using the reindexing construction on the displayed category of isomorphisms.

First we can reindex the category of isomorphisms to get \mathsf {reindex}_{\mathsf {Id} \times F}{\mathopen {}\left (\mathsf {Iso_{D}}\right )\mathclose {}}, a displayed category over \mathcal {D} \times \mathcal {C}. Then using the observation that product categories arise as total categories, we can invoke the displayed total category construction to repackage the data of \mathsf {reindex}_{\mathsf {Id} \times F}{\mathopen {}\left (\mathsf {Iso_{D}}\right )\mathclose {}} as a category displayed over \mathcal {D}, which we call \mathsf {IsoFiber_{F}}.

\mathsf {IsoFiber_{F}} has the universal property that a global section of it comprises the same data as a section of F. That is, a section of \mathsf {IsoFiber_{F}} gives the ingredients to construct a functor G : \mathcal {D} \to \mathcal {C} such that F \circ G \cong \mathsf {Id}.

Given a displayed category \overline {\mathcal {C}} over a category \mathcal {C} and a functor F : \mathcal {D} \to \mathcal {C}, the reindexing of \overline {\mathcal {C}} along F is a displayed category over \mathcal {D}. It is simply the portion of \overline {\mathcal {C}} over the image of F.
Given a category \mathcal {C}, we define a displayed category \mathsf {Iso_{C}} over \mathcal {C} \times \mathcal {C} whose objects describe isomorphisms between the two objects in the base category.

A category \mathcal {C} consists of
A type of objects \mathcal {C}_{0}
For each pair of objects x , y : \mathcal {C}_{0} a set of morphisms \mathcal {C} {\mathopen {}\left (x , y\right )\mathclose {}}. We may simply write a moprhism with an arrow, denote f : \mathcal {C} {\mathopen {}\left (x , y\right )\mathclose {}} as f : x \to y or x \overset {f}{\to } y or similar
A composition operation on morphisms. For f : x \to y and g : y \to z, there is a morphism f \star g : x \to z
For each x : \mathcal {c}_{0}, an identity morphism \mathsf {id}_{x} : x \to x
Left-unitality of composition: for all f : x \to y, an equality \mathsf {idL}_{f} : \mathsf {id}_{x} \star f = f
Right-unitality of composition: for all f : x \to y, an equality \mathsf {idR}_{f} : f \star \mathsf {id}_{y} = f
Associativity of composition: for all f : x \to y, g : y \to z, h : z \to w, an equality \mathsf {assoc}_{f , g , h} : {\mathopen {}\left (f \star {\mathopen {}\left (g \star h\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}} = {\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (f \star g\right )\mathclose {}} \star h\right )\mathclose {}}
Concretely, the definition above is meant to model the one used in the Cubical standard libary [cubicalagdalib].

However, the notion of category is flexible. Depending on the context, we may be talking of small , locally small, wild, or any other kind of category that may augment which things we require to be (homotopy) sets, which things we require to be small types, etc. For the most part, the same idea of a category will apply across all of these settings.
